The Black iguana (Ctenosaura similis) is among the largest-bodied lizards within its genus, with adults attaining a substantial maximum recorded body mass. Field studies conducted on the Pacific coast of Costa Rica have documented that the ultimate wet weight achieved by fully-grown individuals approaches 1034 grams [Wwi = 1034 grams], a size that places them near the upper limit for iguanine lizards in Central America. This considerable adult mass is acquired through a protracted juvenile growth phase that is strongly influenced by thermal conditions in the sun-exposed rocky habitats they occupy. Neonates as they emerge from the egg are impressively diminutive by comparison; the initial wet weight at birth is approximately 9 grams [Wwb = approximately 9 grams], a value that underscores the dramatic size increase required before reaching reproductive maturity. This roughly hundred-fold difference between neonatal and adult mass is a defining feature of the life history strategy observed across many larger iguanid species.

The incubation period for Ctenosaura similis embryos is exquisitely sensitive to the thermal regime of the subterranean nest chamber. In controlled laboratory trials, eggs incubated at a constant 30 °C [T = 30 °C] exhibit a predictable developmental schedule, with pipping and successful emergence of the yolk-sac larva occurring after a relatively brief interval of 90 days [ab = 90 days]. This comparatively short duration of embryonic development, when benchmarked against the prolonged incubation periods of certain tropical crocodilians, likely reflects the elevated metabolic demands placed upon the yolk-dependent embryo at this specific temperature regime. Following eclosion, the lecithotrophic larva phase is fleeting, as the hatchlings rapidly absorb their remaining internal yolk reserves and make the trophic switch to active exogenous feeding within the first few days of life. The timing of this transition is critical for their subsequent survival, as they must quickly locate suitable insect prey in the leaf litter to sustain their rapid early growth.

Regarding the species' maximal reproductive potential under favorable environmental conditions, data gathered from a long-term mark-recapture study in Guanacaste Province provide a detailed picture. Under ambient temperatures that consistently hover around 25 °C [T = 25 °C], nesting females in this population oviposit an average of 30 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 30 eggs per clutch] and deposit a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a reproductive frequency that likely reflects the considerable energetic investment required to produce such a large clutch mass. The combination of large clutch size and annual reproductive frequency gives a substantial annual reproductive output of approximately 30 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 30 eggs per year] for each sexually mature adult female in the population.

Lifespan and the timing of key developmental milestones in this species are also tightly linked to environmental temperature and the social structure of the local population. The oldest documented individuals in wild populations at a typical mean annual temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] have been recorded reaching approximately 60 years [am = approximately 60 years] of age, an extraordinarily long lifespan for a lizard that places Ctenosaura similis at the extreme upper end of squamate longevity records, comparable only to some larger tortoises and tuatara. This remarkable persistence in the wild is facilitated by their relatively low predation risk as adults, owing to their arboreal habits and defensive tail lashing. In contrast, female reproductive maturation occurs considerably earlier in life. The time since metamorphosis from the juvenile stage to the onset of puberty for females has been estimated at approximately 2.5 years since metamorphosis [tp = approximately 2.5 years since metamorphosis], calculated from growth ring annuli data collected at the same thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This relatively rapid sexual maturation, combined with a century-scale lifespan, means that females have an exceptionally long reproductive window.

The basal metabolic rate of Ctenosaura similis has been quantified through open-flow respirometry experiments on quiescent post-absorptive adults. When measured at their preferred body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption recorded was 1.2015 milliliters of oxygen per minute [JOi = 1.2015 milliliters of oxygen per minute]. This metabolic value is notably elevated compared to similarly sized lizards from cooler microhabitats, a finding that underscores the energetic costs associated with maintaining high body temperatures in a heliothermic ectotherm. The elevated metabolic rate at this thermal optimum supports rapid digestion of their largely herbivorous diet and enables the swift growth required to achieve the species' substantial adult body mass. The ability to behaviorally thermoregulate to this precise temperature during the active diurnal period is a cornerstone of their ecology, allowing them to exploit a nutritional niche that is relatively inaccessible to smaller or less thermoregulatively competent sympatric lizards.
